title: CELPIP General Listening — Practice Test 14
instructions: Listen to the audio for each part and answer the questions. Each audio plays once.

parts.title: Problem Solving
parts.description: A conversation in which one person has a problem and seeks help from another.

parts.title: Daily Life Conversation
parts.description: An everyday conversation between two people.

parts.title: Listening for Information
parts.description: An informational talk; listen for specific details.

parts.title: Discussion
parts.description: A discussion among people with different viewpoints.

parts.title: Viewpoints
parts.description: A longer talk presenting one speaker's opinion and reasons.

listeningScripts.title: A Charge for a Missed Appointment
listeningScripts.text: Caller: I've had a bill for forty-five dollars for a missed appointment, but I cancelled it. Reception: Let me look. Which day was the appointment? Caller: The eleventh, at ten past three. Reception: I have it here as a no-show. When did you cancel? Caller: The Friday before. I rang and left a message on the after-hours line. Reception: Ah. That is the difficulty. The after-hours line goes to the answering service, and they pass messages to us the next morning, but only for appointments in the next twenty-four hours. Anything further out than that, they log and we collect on the Monday. And we did have a problem that Monday. The system was down until about eleven. Caller: So the message may have been lost. Reception: It may have been. I can't see it in the log, but the log has a gap in it. Caller: What is the policy meant to be? Reception: Forty-eight hours' notice, and the charge is forty-five dollars. If you rang on the Friday you gave far more than forty-eight hours, so the notice isn't the problem here. The problem is proving the call. Caller: I'd have it on my phone bill. Reception: That would settle it, and it's the easiest way through. A phone bill showing a call to our number on the Friday, and I can waive the charge without going to the practice manager at all. Caller: How do I send it? Reception: Email it to the practice address, with your name and the appointment date in the subject line. Don't reply to the billing email — that goes to a system that doesn't take attachments. Caller: And how long will it take? Reception: I'd do it the same day I see it. But give it three working days before you chase.

listeningScripts.title: A Surprise Sixtieth
listeningScripts.text: A: So. Dad's sixtieth. Are we doing something, or are we pretending we forgot? B: We're doing something. He would never ask for it, and he would be hurt if nothing happened. A: Numbers? B: Thirty. Thirty-five if the cousins come, which they won't, because it's the same weekend as the marathon. A: Thirty, then. Where? The house won't take thirty in October. B: The bowling club does a room for a hundred and twenty, and you bring your own food. A: That is the cheapest thing anybody has ever said to me. What's the catch? B: It's a bowling club. Strip lights and a lino floor. But it is five minutes from his house, and half the people we're inviting don't drive at night any more. A: Then that decides it. The lighting we can fix with lamps. B: Food. I'll do the cooking if you do the invitations. And no speeches. He'll leave if there are speeches. A: One speech. Mine. Two minutes. B: If it runs over two minutes I'm putting the music back on. A: Deal. What about getting him there? He notices everything. B: We tell him we're taking him out to lunch. He gets suspicious about dinner.

listeningScripts.title: Farmers' Market Vendor Briefing
listeningScripts.text: Good morning, and welcome to the vendors' briefing. If you take nothing else away this morning, take these. Set-up runs from six thirty. The gates close to vehicles at seven forty-five, and that one is firm — after that you carry in from the far lot, and the far lot is a long way. Selling starts at eight, and we do not sell before eight, not even to each other, because the customers queuing at the rope can see you. Your stall number is on your permit, and it does not change through the season. If you are going to be away, tell us by the Wednesday and we will fill your space for that week only. It is still yours when you come back. Everything you sell has to be grown, raised, baked or made by you, or on your farm. We do check. A vendor buying at the wholesale market and reselling it here is the one thing that has a permit pulled the same day, with no warning, because it undercuts everybody else on the row and it is a lie to the customer. Scales have to be inspected and stickered, and the sticker has to face the person buying, not you. Samples need gloves, a covered container, and a bin for the sticks. If you are sampling anything with nuts in it, the sign goes on the front of the table where somebody can read it before they take one, not beside the tray. And take your own waste away with you. The bins at the end of the row are for customers. We are charged by weight for those, and last year that bill was two and a half thousand dollars, most of it vendor cardboard.

listeningScripts.title: Prince Edward Island Caps Short-Term Rentals
listeningScripts.text: Prince Edward Island will limit short-term rentals to a property owner's principal residence in three communities, beginning in April. The rule applies in Charlottetown, Summerside and Cavendish, where the province says whole-home listings have grown fastest. An owner renting out a property they do not live in will have to register as a business, and will be capped at ninety nights a year. Housing officials put the number of affected listings at about eleven hundred, and estimate that between two and four hundred homes could return to the long-term rental market. They were careful to say that this is an estimate, and that it depends on what owners choose to do rather than on the rule itself. The tourism industry association called the ninety-night cap arbitrary and warned of a shortage of beds in July and August, when Cavendish doubles in population. The province replied that hotel occupancy in those two months has been below eighty per cent for three years running. Registration opens in February, and enforcement will be complaint-based rather than proactive.

listeningScripts.title: Moving to Shared Desks
listeningScripts.text: Iqbal: The floor is built for ninety, and on the busiest day last month we had fifty-one people in. We are heating and cleaning desks that nobody sits at. Feltham: My team sits together for a reason. Most of them are new, and they learn by overhearing. Scatter them across a floor and you lose the thing that makes a junior useful in six months instead of eighteen. Oyelaran: Nobody is proposing scattering. Neighbourhoods. Each team gets a zone, and inside the zone you sit where you like. Feltham: Then what have we saved? If every team keeps a zone sized for its whole headcount, the floor is the same floor. Iqbal: Zones sized for peak attendance, not for headcount. Yours peaks at eleven of fourteen. Feltham: And on the day I need all fourteen, where do the other three go? Oyelaran: Overflow at the north end. Fourteen desks, bookable, and in practice you would almost never need them. Feltham: Almost never is doing a lot of work in that sentence. The day it fails is a Monday, and it fails for the person who least wants to be told to sit somewhere else. Iqbal: Then let's size the zones for the second-busiest day rather than the average. It costs us a few desks and it takes the failure case away. Oyelaran: I can do that. It is about eight desks across the whole floor. Feltham: And the lockers stay. If people have nowhere to leave things, they will claim a desk anyway, and then we have hot-desking on paper and fixed desks in practice. Iqbal: The lockers stay. That one is cheap.

listeningScripts.title: Banning the Right Turn on Red
listeningScripts.text: A number of cities have started removing the right turn on red — the rule that lets a driver turn after stopping at a red light. It is one of those debates where both sides have a real argument and neither of them is arguing about the same thing. Start with where the rule came from, because it was not introduced for safety. It arrived in the nineteen-seventies as a fuel-saving measure during an oil crisis, on the reasoning that a car idling at a light burns fuel for nothing. That origin matters, because a measure adopted for one reason tends to be defended later on grounds nobody tested at the time. The safety case for removing it is narrower than campaigners often say and stronger than opponents will admit. Crashes on a right turn at red are a small share of all crashes — low single figures. But they are concentrated. They happen at crossings, to people on foot and on bicycles, and disproportionately to the people on foot who move slowest, because the driver is looking left for a gap in the traffic while turning into a space on the right that he never looked at. A small share of crashes that lands almost entirely on one group is not a small problem for that group. The cost of removing it is real too, and it is not fuel. Modern engines idle efficiently enough that the original rationale has largely evaporated. The cost is delay, and delay falls on buses as much as on cars, which is worth saying, because the people arguing for removal usually want better buses as well. So where does that leave it? Remove it at the crossings where the geometry is bad — obstructed sightlines, wide corners that let a driver take the turn fast, heavy foot traffic — and leave it where it does no harm. A blanket ban gives you the fuel argument's shape without its evidence. The problem is specific, and the fix should be specific too.

questions.prompt: Why is the caller telephoning?
options: She was not seen at her appointment time
She has been charged for an appointment she says she cancelled
She has been charged twice for the same visit
She wants to move an appointment to a later date
questions.correctAnswer: She has been charged for an appointment she says she cancelled
questions.explanation: The caller opens with a forty-five dollar bill for a missed appointment which she says she cancelled the Friday before.

questions.prompt: How did the caller cancel?
options: By speaking to reception during the day
By replying to a reminder email
Through the practice's booking website
By leaving a message on the after-hours line
questions.correctAnswer: By leaving a message on the after-hours line
questions.explanation: She rang and left a message on the after-hours line on the Friday before the appointment.

questions.prompt: What does the answering service do with a message about a more distant appointment?
options: It logs the message for the practice to collect on Monday
It passes it on the following morning
It telephones the patient back to confirm
It cancels the appointment directly in the system
questions.correctAnswer: It logs the message for the practice to collect on Monday
questions.explanation: Messages are passed on next morning only for appointments within twenty-four hours; anything further out is logged for the practice to collect on the Monday.

questions.prompt: What went wrong on that Monday?
options: The answering service was closed
Reception was short-staffed
The practice's system was down until about eleven
The message log was deleted by mistake
questions.correctAnswer: The practice's system was down until about eleven
questions.explanation: Reception says the system was down until about eleven that Monday, which is why the log has a gap where the message should be.

questions.prompt: How much notice does the policy require?
options: Twenty-four hours
Forty-eight hours
Three working days
Notice by the Friday before
questions.correctAnswer: Forty-eight hours
questions.explanation: The policy is forty-eight hours' notice with a forty-five dollar charge. A call on the Friday is well beyond that, which is why reception says the notice is not the problem.

questions.prompt: What does reception say the real problem is?
options: That the notice given was too short
That the charge has already been processed
Proving that the call was made
That the after-hours line was the wrong number to ring
questions.correctAnswer: Proving that the call was made
questions.explanation: Reception is explicit that the notice period is not in question — what is missing is proof of the call, because the log has a gap.

questions.prompt: What would settle the matter?
options: A letter from the caller confirming the cancellation
A recording from the answering service
A decision from the practice manager
A phone bill showing the call on the Friday
questions.correctAnswer: A phone bill showing the call on the Friday
questions.explanation: A phone bill showing a call to the practice on the Friday would settle it, and would let reception waive the charge without involving the practice manager.

questions.prompt: Why should the caller not reply to the billing email?
options: That address goes to a system that cannot receive attachments
Billing emails are answered only once a week
The billing office would refer it back anyway
Replies are treated as an acceptance of the charge
questions.correctAnswer: That address goes to a system that cannot receive attachments
questions.explanation: Reception asks for the practice address rather than a reply to the billing email, because the billing email goes to a system that does not take attachments.

questions.prompt: How many people do they expect?
options: About thirty
About thirty-five
About fifteen
They have not decided
questions.correctAnswer: About thirty
questions.explanation: B expects thirty, and thirty-five only if the cousins come — which they will not, because of the marathon.

questions.prompt: Why will the cousins not come?
options: They live too far away
They have not been invited
The date clashes with the marathon
They will be at another birthday
questions.correctAnswer: The date clashes with the marathon
questions.explanation: The party falls on the same weekend as the marathon, which is why B rules the cousins out.

questions.prompt: Why do they choose the bowling club?
options: It is the only room available in October
It is close to their father's house
It has better lighting than the alternatives
It provides the food as well as the room
questions.correctAnswer: It is close to their father's house
questions.explanation: A is won over by the club being five minutes from his house, since half the guests no longer drive at night. The lighting is a drawback they plan to fix with lamps, and the food is brought in.

questions.prompt: What do they agree about speeches?
options: There will be none at all
Each of them will give one
They will decide on the day
There will be one, lasting two minutes
questions.correctAnswer: There will be one, lasting two minutes
questions.explanation: B wants no speeches because their father would leave; A negotiates one two-minute speech, with the music going back on if it runs over.

questions.prompt: How do they plan to get their father there?
options: By asking him to collect something from the club
By telling him it is somebody else's party
By telling him he is being taken out to lunch
By having a neighbour drive him
questions.correctAnswer: By telling him he is being taken out to lunch
questions.explanation: B suggests saying they are taking him out to lunch, because dinner would make him suspicious.

questions.prompt: When do the gates close to vehicles?
options: At half past six
At eight o'clock
At seven o'clock
At a quarter to eight
questions.correctAnswer: At a quarter to eight
questions.explanation: Set-up runs from six thirty and the gates close to vehicles at seven forty-five; selling then begins at eight.

questions.prompt: What happens to a vendor's space when they are away?
options: It is filled for that week only
It is reassigned for the rest of the season
It is left empty until they return
It is offered to the vendor beside them
questions.correctAnswer: It is filled for that week only
questions.explanation: Given notice by the Wednesday, the market fills the space for that week only — the stall number stays with the vendor for the season.

questions.prompt: What has a permit pulled the same day?
options: Selling before eight o'clock
Using scales without a sticker
Reselling goods bought at the wholesale market
Leaving cardboard in the customer bins
questions.correctAnswer: Reselling goods bought at the wholesale market
questions.explanation: Buying at the wholesale market and reselling is the one offence with no warning attached, because it undercuts the row and misleads the customer.

questions.prompt: Which way must the scale's sticker face?
options: Towards the vendor
Towards the customer
Towards the aisle
It may face either way
questions.correctAnswer: Towards the customer
questions.explanation: The sticker has to face the person buying rather than the vendor, so the customer can see the scale has been inspected.

questions.prompt: Where must a warning about nuts be displayed?
options: Beside the sample tray
On the covered container
On the permit at the stall
On the front of the table
questions.correctAnswer: On the front of the table
questions.explanation: The sign goes on the front of the table where it can be read before somebody takes a sample, rather than beside the tray where it would be read too late.

questions.prompt: Why must vendors take their own waste away?
options: The market is charged by weight for the customer bins
The bins are emptied only once a week
Cardboard cannot be recycled at the site
Waste attracts animals overnight
questions.correctAnswer: The market is charged by weight for the customer bins
questions.explanation: The end-of-row bins are for customers and are charged by weight — last year's bill was two and a half thousand dollars, most of it vendor cardboard.

questions.prompt: What is being restricted?
options: All short-term rentals across the province
Hotels operating outside the summer season
Renting out a property the owner does not live in
The building of new holiday properties
questions.correctAnswer: Renting out a property the owner does not live in
questions.explanation: The rule limits short-term rentals to an owner's principal residence in three communities; letting a property you do not live in means registering as a business and a ninety-night cap.

questions.prompt: Where does the rule apply?
options: Across the whole province
In Charlottetown, Summerside and Cavendish
In Cavendish only
In every community with a hotel
questions.correctAnswer: In Charlottetown, Summerside and Cavendish
questions.explanation: The three named communities are where the province says whole-home listings have grown fastest.

questions.prompt: What were housing officials careful to say?
options: The three communities asked for the rule themselves
Enforcement will not begin until the following year
The rule may be extended to other communities
The number of homes returning depends on what owners decide to do
questions.correctAnswer: The number of homes returning depends on what owners decide to do
questions.explanation: Officials gave two to four hundred homes as an estimate and stressed that it turns on owners' choices rather than on the rule itself.

questions.prompt: What was the tourism association's objection?
options: The cap is arbitrary and beds will run short in summer
Registration opens too late to be useful
Complaint-based enforcement will not work
Cavendish was wrongly included in the rule
questions.correctAnswer: The cap is arbitrary and beds will run short in summer
questions.explanation: The association called the ninety-night cap arbitrary and warned of a bed shortage in July and August, when Cavendish doubles in population.

questions.prompt: How did the province answer that?
options: The cap will be reviewed after the first summer
Hotel occupancy in those months has been under eighty per cent
Cavendish has more beds than it needs already
The tourism figures have not been verified
questions.correctAnswer: Hotel occupancy in those months has been under eighty per cent
questions.explanation: The province's reply was that hotel occupancy in July and August has been below eighty per cent for three years running.

questions.prompt: What does Iqbal point to at the start?
options: A floor built for ninety with fifty-one people at its busiest
A rise in heating and cleaning costs this year
A shortage of desks on the busiest days
Complaints from staff about the current layout
questions.correctAnswer: A floor built for ninety with fifty-one people at its busiest
questions.explanation: Iqbal's opening figure is a floor built for ninety against a busiest day of fifty-one, with heating and cleaning going to desks nobody uses.

questions.prompt: What is Feltham's objection?
options: Her team would refuse to move desks
Shared desks spread illness through a floor
Her team needs equipment that cannot be moved
New staff learn by overhearing the people around them
questions.correctAnswer: New staff learn by overhearing the people around them
questions.explanation: Feltham argues her mostly new team learns by overhearing, and that scattering them costs the difference between a junior being useful in six months and in eighteen.

questions.prompt: What does Oyelaran propose?
options: Keeping fixed desks for new staff only
A zone for each team, with free choice of desk inside it
Closing part of the floor entirely
Booking every desk in advance through an app
questions.correctAnswer: A zone for each team, with free choice of desk inside it
questions.explanation: Oyelaran's neighbourhoods keep each team in a zone while letting people sit anywhere within it, which he offers as an answer to the scattering objection.

questions.prompt: What is Feltham's response to the zones?
options: Zones would separate her team from the others
The north end is too far from her team
If each zone matches a team's headcount, nothing is saved
Teams would not respect the zone boundaries
questions.correctAnswer: If each zone matches a team's headcount, nothing is saved
questions.explanation: Feltham points out that zones sized for whole headcounts leave the floor exactly as big as it was, which is what prompts Iqbal to size them by peak attendance instead.

questions.prompt: How does Iqbal say zones should be sized?
options: By the average attendance across a month
By the size of each team's equipment
By giving every team the same number of desks
By how many actually attend at peak, not by headcount
questions.correctAnswer: By how many actually attend at peak, not by headcount
questions.explanation: Iqbal proposes sizing by peak attendance rather than headcount, noting that Feltham's team of fourteen peaks at eleven.

questions.prompt: What is Feltham's worry about the overflow desks?
options: The day the arrangement fails will be the worst day for it to fail
Fourteen desks are not enough for the whole floor
Booking a desk takes too long in the morning
The north end is used by another team already
questions.correctAnswer: The day the arrangement fails will be the worst day for it to fail
questions.explanation: Feltham objects to the phrase almost never: the day it fails is a Monday, and it fails for the person least willing to be sent elsewhere.

questions.prompt: What do they agree on?
options: Keeping the floor as it is for another year
Removing the overflow desks altogether
Sizing the zones for the second-busiest day, at a cost of about eight desks
Sizing the zones for the average day
questions.correctAnswer: Sizing the zones for the second-busiest day, at a cost of about eight desks
questions.explanation: Iqbal proposes the second-busiest day rather than the average, which removes the failure case; Oyelaran costs it at about eight desks across the floor.

questions.prompt: What does Feltham insist on keeping?
options: Her team's existing desks
The lockers
The north end overflow
A fixed desk for each new member of staff
questions.correctAnswer: The lockers
questions.explanation: Feltham's condition is that the lockers stay, since people with nowhere to leave things will claim a desk anyway and leave the office hot-desking in name only.

questions.prompt: Why was the right turn on red introduced?
options: To reduce congestion at busy crossings
To save fuel during an oil crisis
To make crossings safer for drivers turning
To match the rule in neighbouring countries
questions.correctAnswer: To save fuel during an oil crisis
questions.explanation: The rule arrived in the nineteen-seventies as a fuel-saving measure during an oil crisis, on the reasoning that idling burns fuel for nothing. It was not introduced for safety.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker say that origin matters?
options: The oil crisis has not recurred since
Fuel savings were never actually measured
A measure adopted for one reason is later defended on untested grounds
The rule was meant to be temporary
questions.correctAnswer: A measure adopted for one reason is later defended on untested grounds
questions.explanation: The speaker's point is that a rule adopted for one reason tends to be defended later on grounds nobody tested when it was brought in.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say about crashes on a right turn at red?
options: They are few in number but fall on people walking and cycling
They are the largest single category of urban crash
They have risen sharply since the nineteen-seventies
They occur mostly between two vehicles
questions.correctAnswer: They are few in number but fall on people walking and cycling
questions.explanation: Such crashes are a small share of all crashes — low single figures — but concentrated at crossings on people on foot and on bicycles, and especially on those who move slowest.

questions.prompt: Why does the driver fail to see them?
options: He is watching the light rather than the road
The crossing is behind him by the time he turns
He expects the crossing to be empty at a red light
He is looking left for a gap while turning to the right
questions.correctAnswer: He is looking left for a gap while turning to the right
questions.explanation: The driver looks left for a gap in the traffic while turning into a space on the right that he never looked at.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say the real cost of removal is?
options: Extra fuel burned while idling
Delay, which falls on buses as well as cars
The cost of changing the signs
Longer routes for delivery vehicles
questions.correctAnswer: Delay, which falls on buses as well as cars
questions.explanation: Modern engines idle efficiently enough that the fuel rationale has largely evaporated; the cost is delay, and it falls on buses as much as on cars — awkwardly for the people who want both.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker conclude?
options: Remove it everywhere, since the harm is concentrated
Keep it everywhere until better evidence exists
Replace it with a longer crossing signal
Remove it where the geometry is bad and leave it elsewhere
questions.correctAnswer: Remove it where the geometry is bad and leave it elsewhere
questions.explanation: The conclusion is a specific fix for a specific problem: remove it at crossings with obstructed sightlines, wide fast corners or heavy foot traffic, and leave it where it does no harm.
